title: Residency review, housing squeeze and doctors' strikes
summary:
Brussels is examining a complaint over Spain's immigrant regularisation, while an overseas voting deadline arrives. We cover housing affordability, tighter lending, doctors' strikes and a remarkable archaeological discovery in Murcia.

Enjoying Spain Daily? Support us: https://buymeacoffee.com/spanified

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Spain expected half a million applications. More than double arrived.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: More than a million, in fact. And now Brussels is looking at how Spain did it. wow

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Hold on. Could Brussels actually challenge the process?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That matters to everyone still waiting for their papers.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Good morning! It's Wednesday, the twenty-eighth of October, and this is Spain Daily, from Spanified dot com!

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: I'm Inna, here with Dima. Today: doctors' strikes, and an ancient wall whose location makes its enormous size puzzling.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: We'll reach that mystery in Murcia later. First, Brussels and Spain's regularisation, the route to residency for people without papers.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: El Mundo reports that the European Commission is examining Junts's complaint about Spain's regularisation by Royal Decree. Almost one point two million applications arrived, against an expected half a million. Applications closed on June thirtieth, and many decisions remain pending.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Junts argues the government should have passed a law in the Cortes, Spain's parliament, and says Spain breached EU rules. The Commission has not ruled out a future infringement procedure, a formal case over an alleged breach of EU law.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oof. If you are waiting for residency, that is one more worry.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: But Inna, does a complaint from a political party mean the Commission will actually open that case? good question

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Not yet. The Commission only said it will examine the complaint. It did not rule out a case later.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And people who are already regularised? Could they lose anything?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The announced step is an examination of Spain's measures, not a decision cancelling anyone's residency. right Applications are still being resolved.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: So for now, the real wait is still the decision on each file.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Another legal deadline affects Spaniards abroad. El Mundo says ministers must deliver the list of affected overseas voters today by three in the afternoon. Voting rights are suspended for more than a hundred and sixty thousand beneficiaries of the grandchildren's law, the Ley de Nietos, who lack proof of descent from forced exiles. The election is November twenty-ninth.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Wait, could missing the deadline stop everyone abroad from voting?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The Supreme Court has ruled out suspending the entire overseas vote. Ministers could face criminal liability and fines over the list.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Interesting. The government spokesperson says the deadline will be met, but Foreign Affairs says some consulates can't finish in time.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Buying outside Madrid doesn't necessarily offer an affordable escape. El Confidencial reports Tinsa's finding: in eighty-one percent of surrounding municipalities, buying takes more than forty-five percent of disposable income. The squeeze also affects much of Barcelona's commuter belt. Price rises around Madrid have slowed, but prices are still climbing.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Torrejón de Ardoz, a town in Madrid province, led the rises! So moving out is not the cheap escape anymore.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Renters get something different now. Public land, private builders, rents tied to income.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Veinte Minutos reports that the cabinet approved about two hundred million euros yesterday for around two thousand five hundred affordable rentals. Private developers would build on Casa forty-seven public land, with rents tied to household income. The related housing decree still needs Congress's approval.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Contracts are long, too, and can be extended for decades. oh nice That is a long time for a renter.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: But two thousand five hundred homes? Across all of Spain? That is small.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Small, yes. But they are spread across provinces like Málaga, Sevilla and Valencia. For those tenants it matters.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Inna, who faces the bigger borrowing squeeze now: mortgage applicants or people seeking consumer credit?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Consumer credit faces particular tightening, El Mundo reports from the European Central Bank's lending survey. Banks expect tougher criteria for household borrowing through December, including mortgages. Higher funding costs have made new loans less favourable. Rising interest rates drove weaker demand, with home-purchase borrowing falling most sharply.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Huh. For a buyer, that is one more wall.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: And the market expects at least one more rate rise before next year. So it may get worse.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For retirement income, Veinte Minutos reports an average pension of almost sixteen hundred euros a month in October.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The average in the self-employed scheme is much lower. Overall pension spending rose as inflation-linked increases and the first baby-boom retirements fed through.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Hm. Only about one thousand sixty euros for the self-employed? That is far below the average.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The general regime pays a lot more. That is a big gap.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Why build enormous defences around a city already protected by a plateau?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's the mystery at La Almoloya, an ancient Argaric city in Pliego, Murcia. El País reports that archaeologists uncovered a wall up to seven metres wide, with towers. The city is roughly four thousand years old, and its natural defences make the fortification especially puzzling.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Apparently, being on a difficult-to-reach plateau wasn't enough reassurance. Do the archaeologists have an explanation?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: They see evidence of concentrated power and threats the inhabitants felt they faced. Exactly why such strong walls were needed remains a mystery.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: El Mundo reports that the government is working to prevent further violence around the November eleventh housing general strike. Riots have occurred in Barcelona and Bilbao. The government distinguishes those responsible from the unions calling the strike and expects the strike to proceed normally.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: It also admits other groups could try to exploit the strike. And PP and Vox are making insecurity a campaign issue.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Meanwhile, El Diario reports a planned November twelfth Congress vote on two housing decrees, although the date remains unconfirmed. Their legal deadline expires November fourteenth. PP, Vox and Junts defeated earlier versions.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Waiting keeps the measures in force longer. But it puts the vote right before the campaign starts.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And earlier versions were defeated, so the outcome is far from certain.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: On jobs, El País reports that unemployment rose to about ten point two percent in July to September. Employment nevertheless reached a record. Job creation slowed, and the quarterly gain was the weakest for a third quarter in seven years.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: How can employment reach a record while unemployment rises?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Because more people are looking for work too. The number of unemployed grew by more than the number of new jobs.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: El Diario reports a European Commission proposal to expand Frontex, the EU border agency, to thirty thousand agents. That includes a seventeen-thousand-agent rapid reaction force. Frontex would gain a larger deportation role, including transfers to planned centres outside Europe. The proposal has not been adopted.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Would the change involve carrying out returns, rather than just providing more staff?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Yes. Frontex would get more capacity to organise and carry out returns, including in third countries. The article calls this the most controversial part.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Madrid doctors begin a three-day strike today, running through October thirtieth, El Diario reports. Further rounds run through December. Regional action continues elsewhere over pay and twenty-four-hour shifts. Unions postponed the national strike because of the early election, but regional disputes may still disrupt public healthcare.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Who can deliver the changes doctors are demanding: the national government or regional health departments?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Responsibilities are shared, but regions can independently implement improvements. The current action targets regional departments, so the national postponement doesn't remove local disruption.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Finally, Veinte Minutos reports that more than four thousand self-employed Uber Eats riders will become employees of Quinde Crew, the company taking over Uber Eats' delivery division, from November thirtieth.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The agreement with UGT and Comisiones Obreras also improves conditions for more than eight thousand riders. A commission will monitor compliance.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That's thousands of riders moving to employee status. What else is in the deal?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: A permanent commission will talk about pay, working time and algorithms. And both sides want a sector-wide agreement.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: So a contract, plus a seat at the table. More than a new label.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Coming up: Madrid's doctors' strikes through October thirtieth, the housing strike on November eleventh, a possible Congress vote the day after, and the election on November twenty-ninth.
